module.title: Obligations & Rules: Must, Mustn't & Have to
module.objective: Express rules, obligations, and prohibitions in public places and school using 'must', 'mustn't', and 'have to'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Rules Around Us
subModules.grammarFocus: Must, Mustn't, Have to, Don't have to — expressing obligations, prohibitions, and lack of obligation
subModules.vocabularyFocus: School rules, public place regulations, everyday obligations and prohibitions

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a short passage about rules at a school and a public swimming pool. You will learn to understand sentences with 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', and 'don't have to'. These words help us talk about things we need to do (obligations), things we cannot do (prohibitions), and things that are optional (not necessary). By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading signs, notices, and short texts about rules in English. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Modal verbs 'must' and 'mustn't' for strong obligations and prohibitions; 'have to / has to' for external obligations; 'don't have to / doesn't have to' for lack of obligation. All followed by the base form of the verb.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words related to rules, schools, and public places: helmet, uniform, corridor, library, queue, deadline, permission, rule, fine, sign, allowed, forbidden, locker.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for key modal verbs (must, mustn't, have to, don't have to) to quickly identify what is required, what is prohibited, and what is optional in a text.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about rules and obligations.
Identify specific rules, obligations, and prohibitions mentioned in the passage.
Recognize the difference between 'mustn't' (prohibition) and 'don't have to' (not necessary) in context.
Match modal verbs to their correct meaning when reading signs and notices.
Build confidence reading everyday English texts about rules at school and in public places.

contextWarmup.prompt: You see a sign at a swimming pool that says: 'You must shower before entering the pool.' What does this sign mean?
options: You need to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
You can take a shower if you want, but it is not necessary.
You must not take a shower at the pool.
contextWarmup.explanation: Great job! The word 'must' tells us this is a strong rule — it is required. You need to shower before you enter the pool. It is not optional!

rules: When you see 'must' + verb in a text, it means something is very important or required. Example: 'You must wear a helmet.' = It is a rule. You need to wear a helmet.
When you see 'mustn't' + verb, it means something is NOT allowed — it is a prohibition. Example: 'You mustn't run in the corridor.' = Running is forbidden. Do not run!
When you see 'have to' or 'has to' + verb, it means there is an obligation, often because of an external rule. Example: 'She has to arrive on time.' = The school requires her to be on time.

When you see 'don't have to' or 'doesn't have to' + verb, it means something is NOT necessary — you can choose. Example: 'You don't have to bring lunch.' = Bringing lunch is optional. You can bring it or not.
Important reading tip: 'mustn't' and 'don't have to' look similar but have very different meanings! Always check carefully: mustn't = forbidden, don't have to = not necessary.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Common Beginner Pitfall: Mustn't vs. Don't Have To
commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners confuse 'mustn't' with 'don't have to'. Remember: 'mustn't' means it is FORBIDDEN — you cannot do it. 'Don't have to' means it is NOT NECESSARY — you can do it if you want, but you don't need to. When reading, pay close attention to which phrase is used because the meaning is completely different!
commonTrap.wrong: Reading 'You don't have to park here' and thinking it means parking is forbidden.
commonTrap.correct: 'You don't have to park here' means parking here is not necessary — you can park somewhere else if you prefer. If parking is forbidden, the sign says 'You mustn't park here.'

sections.title: Reading Passage: New Student, New Rules

content.context: Rina is a new student at Greenfield International School. On her first day, her teacher, Mr. Adams, gives the class a list of school rules. Rina also visits the public swimming pool near her house after school. Read about the rules she learns in both places.
content.text:
Today is Rina's first day at Greenfield International School. Mr. Adams, her teacher, says: 'Welcome, everyone! Let me tell you about our school rules. First, all students must wear their uniform every day. You mustn't wear jeans or T-shirts. Second, you must be quiet in the library. You mustn't use your phone there. Third, you have to finish your homework before the deadline. If you return a library book late, you have to pay a fine. But don't worry — you don't have to bring lunch from home. You can buy food at the school cafeteria.'

After school, Rina goes to the swimming pool near her house. She sees a big sign at the entrance. It says: 'Pool Rules: You must shower before entering the pool. You mustn't run near the pool. Children under 12 must be with an adult. You don't have to bring your own towel — we have towels here.' Rina smiles. 'There are rules everywhere!' she thinks.

highlights.note: Strong obligation: wearing a uniform is required by the school.
Prohibition: jeans and T-shirts are not allowed at school.
Strong rule: silence is required in the library.
Prohibition: using phones in the library is forbidden.
'Have to' shows an external obligation — the school requires it.
An obligation as a consequence: you must pay money if a book is late.
Not necessary: bringing lunch is optional, not required.
Strong rule at the pool: showering is required before swimming.
Prohibition: running near the pool is dangerous and not allowed.
Not necessary: bringing a towel is optional because the pool provides them.
Special clothes that students wear at school.
The last day or time to finish something.
Money you must pay as a penalty for breaking a rule.
A board or notice with information or rules.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Rina learns about rules at her new school and at a public swimming pool.
Rina does not like the rules at her new school.
Rina goes swimming with her teacher, Mr. Adams.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about the rules Rina learns in two places: her new school (Greenfield International School) and the public swimming pool near her house. The text describes what she must do, what she mustn't do, and what she doesn't have to do.

detailQuestions.prompt: According to the school rules, what mustn't students wear?
detailQuestions.explanation: Mr. Adams says: 'You mustn't wear jeans or T-shirts.' The word 'mustn't' tells us these clothes are not allowed at school. Students must wear their uniform instead.

detailQuestions.prompt: What happens if a student returns a library book late?
options: The student has to pay a fine.
The student mustn't go to the library again.
The student doesn't have to do anything.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'If you return a library book late, you have to pay a fine.' This means paying a fine (a small amount of money) is an obligation when a book is returned after the deadline.

detailQuestions.prompt: At the swimming pool, do visitors have to bring their own towel?
options: No, they don't have to. The pool has towels.
Yes, they must bring a towel from home.
Yes, they have to buy a towel at the pool.
detailQuestions.explanation: The sign at the pool says: 'You don't have to bring your own towel — we have towels here.' This means bringing a towel is NOT necessary. The pool provides towels for visitors.

detailQuestions.prompt: Who must be with children under 12 at the swimming pool?
detailQuestions.explanation: The pool rules state: 'Children under 12 must be with an adult.' This is a strong obligation — young children cannot go to the pool alone.

questions.question: In the passage, Mr. Adams says students must be quiet in the library. What does 'must be quiet' mean?
options: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
It is a suggestion — students can be quiet if they want.
It is not important — students can talk if they want.
questions.answer: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong obligation. When Mr. Adams says 'You must be quiet in the library,' he means it is a rule that all students need to follow. Being quiet in the library is required, not optional.

questions.question: The passage says: 'You don't have to bring lunch from home.' What does this mean?
options: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
Bringing lunch from home is forbidden. You must buy food at school.
You must bring lunch from home every day.
questions.answer: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
questions.explanation: 'Don't have to' means something is NOT necessary — it is optional. Students can bring lunch if they want, but they can also buy food at the school cafeteria. It is their choice!

questions.question: Which of these is a PROHIBITION (something you cannot do) mentioned in the passage?
options: You mustn't run near the pool.
You don't have to bring your own towel.
You have to finish your homework.
questions.answer: You mustn't run near the pool.
questions.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a prohibition — something that is forbidden. Running near the pool is not allowed because it is dangerous. 'Don't have to' (option B) means not necessary, and 'have to' (option C) means an obligation, not a prohibition.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to which place?
questions.answer: The library
questions.explanation: In the passage, Mr. Adams talks about the library rules. He says: 'You must be quiet in the library. You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to the library, which was mentioned in the sentence before.

questions.question: A sign says: 'You must shower before entering the pool.' Which sentence has the SAME meaning?
options: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
You don't have to shower. It is your choice.
You mustn't shower at the pool.
questions.answer: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
questions.explanation: Both 'must' and 'have to' can express obligation. 'You must shower' and 'You have to take a shower' have the same meaning here — showering before swimming is a rule that everyone needs to follow.

questions.question: At the end of the passage, Rina thinks: 'There are rules everywhere!' Why does she think this?
options: Because she finds rules both at school and at the swimming pool.
Because she does not like any rules.
Because there are no rules at the swimming pool.
questions.answer: Because she finds rules both at school and at the swimming pool.
questions.explanation: Rina learns rules at two different places on the same day — at her new school and at the swimming pool. She notices that rules exist in many places in daily life, so she thinks 'There are rules everywhere!'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence about the school rules in the passage:
options: Students have to finish their homework before the deadline.
Students don't have to wear a uniform.
questions.answer: Students have to finish their homework before the deadline.
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states: 'You have to finish your homework before the deadline.' This is an obligation. Option B is wrong because students MUST wear a uniform. Option C is wrong because 'mustn't finish' would mean finishing homework is forbidden, which does not make sense.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'You mustn't eat here' and 'You don't have to eat here'?
options: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
'Don't have to eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Mustn't eat' means eating is optional.
questions.answer: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
questions.explanation: This is a very important difference! 'Mustn't' = prohibition (you cannot do it). 'Don't have to' = not necessary (you can choose). 'You mustn't eat here' means eating is NOT allowed. 'You don't have to eat here' means you can eat here if you want, but it is not required.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Understanding School Rules and Obligations

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a teacher explaining school rules to a new student on the first day of school. Listen carefully for the words 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', and 'don't have to'. These words tell us about obligations (things we need to do), prohibitions (things we cannot do), and things that are not necessary. Pay attention to the speaker's tone of voice. When a teacher says 'mustn't', the voice is often firm and serious. When they say 'don't have to', the voice is more relaxed because it means something is optional, not required.
learningObjectives: Identify when a speaker uses 'must' to express a strong obligation or rule.
Recognize 'mustn't' in spoken English as a prohibition, meaning something is not allowed.
Understand the difference between 'have to' (it is necessary) and 'don't have to' (it is not necessary) when listening to natural speech.
Catch key details about specific rules mentioned in a conversation about school or public places.

keyPhrases.note: Used to express a strong rule or obligation. The speaker is telling you it is required.

keyPhrases.phrase: You mustn't use phones in class.
keyPhrases.meaning: Kamu tidak boleh menggunakan HP di kelas.
keyPhrases.note: Used to express a prohibition. This means it is not allowed. 'Mustn't' is a strong 'no'.

keyPhrases.phrase: You have to keep them in your bags.
keyPhrases.note: Used to express a necessary action or obligation, similar to 'must' but slightly less formal.

keyPhrases.phrase: You don't have to wear it on Saturday.
keyPhrases.meaning: Kamu tidak harus memakainya di hari Sabtu.
keyPhrases.note: Used to say something is NOT necessary. It is your choice. This is different from 'mustn't' which means not allowed.
A common rule in places like libraries, hospitals, or during exams. 'Be quiet' means do not make noise.
This prohibits loud talking. Notice 'mustn't' is followed by the base verb without 'to'.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, the 't' at the end of 'must' is often dropped or unreleased before the 'w' sound. Also, 'you' reduces to 'yuh' and 'your' reduces to 'yer'.
In natural speech, 'mustn't' often sounds like 'mussnt' with the second 't' almost silent. The word blends quickly, so listen for the nasal 'n' sound to catch the negative.

connectedSpeech.slow: Do we have to wear uniforms?
connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'have to' becomes 'hafta' with the 'v' changing to an 'f' sound. 'Do we' blends together into 'dwee'. This is very common in everyday English.

connectedSpeech.slow: You don't have to wear it.
connectedSpeech.note: The 't' in 'don't' is often dropped before the 'h' in 'have'. 'Have to' again becomes 'hafta'. Listen for 'don' hafta' as one smooth phrase.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Rules & Obligations at School and Public Places

content.summary: In this lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about rules, obligations, and things that are not allowed. You will use 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', 'has to', 'don't have to', and 'doesn't have to'. These words help you talk about rules at school, at the library, and in other public places. Pay attention to the sentence formulas and punctuation rules below.

blueprintItems.title: Writing a Strong Rule with 'Must'
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + must + base verb + rest of sentence.
blueprintItems.example: Students must wear uniforms at school.

blueprintItems.title: Writing a Prohibition with 'Mustn't'
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + mustn't + base verb + rest of sentence.
blueprintItems.example: You mustn't run in the corridor.

blueprintItems.title: Writing an Obligation with 'Have to / Has to'
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have to / has to + base verb + rest of sentence.
blueprintItems.example: She has to arrive on time every day.

blueprintItems.title: Writing About No Obligation with 'Don't have to / Doesn't have to'
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + don't have to / doesn't have to + base verb + rest of sentence.
blueprintItems.example: You don't have to bring lunch to school.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use the base form of the verb after 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', and 'has to'. Never add '-s', '-ing', or '-ed' to the verb.
mechanicsRules.why: Modal verbs like 'must' and phrases like 'have to' are always followed by the base form of the verb. We do not change the verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'has to' only with he, she, and it. Use 'have to' with I, you, we, and they.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He have to finish his homework.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He has to finish his homework.
mechanicsRules.why: For third person singular subjects (he, she, it), we change 'have' to 'has'. This is a grammar rule for 'have to'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Write 'mustn't' as one word with an apostrophe. Do not write 'must not' as 'mustn t' or 'must'nt'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You mustn t use your phone.
mechanicsRules.why: The apostrophe in 'mustn't' replaces the missing letter 'o' from 'must not'. It must be placed correctly between 'n' and 't'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Start every sentence with a capital letter and end it with a period (full stop).
mechanicsRules.badExample: students must be quiet in the library
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Students must be quiet in the library.
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a period. This is a basic punctuation rule.

sampleSentences.focus: must + base verb for a strong rule

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Rules & Obligations – Must, Mustn't & Have to

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise talking about rules, obligations, and things that are not allowed. You will use 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', and 'don't have to' to describe rules at school, in the library, at the hospital, and other public places. Pay special attention to how you stress the modal verbs to sound clear and natural.
content.audioGuidance: When you say 'must' or 'mustn't', make the word short and strong. Say 'MUST' with a clear /m/ sound and a short /ʌ/ vowel. For 'mustn't', be careful: the 't' in the middle is almost silent – say it like 'MUSS-nt'. For 'have to', in natural speech we often say 'HAF-tuh', not 'HAVE-TOO'. Use falling intonation at the end of rule statements like 'You must wear a uniform.' Use rising intonation for yes/no questions like 'Do I have to bring my book?'

pillars.name: Modal Stress & Clarity
pillars.target: Clear pronunciation of must, mustn't, have to
pillars.explanation: Practise saying 'must' /mʌst/, 'mustn't' /ˈmʌs.ənt/, and 'have to' /ˈhæf.tə/. These words carry the meaning of the rule, so they need to be clear and strong in your sentence.

pillars.name: Falling Intonation for Rules
pillars.target: Use falling tone when stating rules and obligations
pillars.explanation: When you tell someone a rule, your voice should go DOWN at the end. For example: 'You must wear a seatbelt. ↘' This falling intonation shows that you are giving a firm statement, not asking a question.

pillars.name: Rising Intonation for Questions
pillars.target: Use rising tone for yes/no questions about rules
pillars.explanation: When you ask a yes/no question about a rule, your voice should go UP at the end. For example: 'Do I have to bring my ID? ↗' This rising intonation tells the listener you are asking, not telling.

pillars.name: Sentence Rhythm & Linking
pillars.explanation: In natural speech, words connect together. 'Have to' sounds like 'haf-tuh'. 'Must I' links to sound like 'mus-tai'. Practise linking these words so your speech flows smoothly and sounds natural.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Both 'must' and 'mustn't' keep the stress on the first syllable. The negative ending '-n't' is short and soft. Be careful not to add an extra vowel sound – say 'MUSS-nt', not 'MUS-suh-NOT'.
When 'have' is used alone, we say /hæv/ with a /v/ sound. But in 'have to', the /v/ changes to /f/ and 'to' becomes a weak 'tuh'. So 'have to' sounds like 'HAF-tuh'. The stress stays on 'HAF'.
'Uniform' has stress on the first syllable: 'U-ni-form'. But 'obligation' has stress on the third syllable: 'ob-li-GA-tion'. Notice how the stress moves to a different position in longer words.
'Allowed' has stress on the second syllable: 'al-LOWED'. 'Forbidden' also has stress on the second syllable: 'for-BID-den'. Both words relate to rules, and both stress the middle part.

drills.targetText: You must wear a uniform at school.
drills.phonetic: /juː mʌst weər ə ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːm ət skuːl/
drills.focus: Clear pronunciation of 'must' and falling intonation for a rule statement
drills.hint: Say 'must' with a short, strong /ʌ/ sound. Let your voice fall at the end of the sentence to show it is a firm rule.

drills.targetText: You mustn't run in the hallway.
drills.hint: Say 'mustn't' as two syllables: 'MUSS-nt'. The 't' in the middle is almost silent. Do not say 'must-uh-not'.

drills.targetText: I have to do my homework every day.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ ˈhæf.tə duː maɪ ˈhəʊm.wɜːk ˈev.ri deɪ/
drills.hint: Remember: 'have to' sounds like 'HAF-tuh' in natural speech. The /v/ changes to /f/ before 'to'.

drills.targetText: Do I have to bring my passport?
drills.focus: Rising intonation for a yes/no question about obligation
drills.hint: This is a yes/no question, so your voice should rise at the end: 'passport? ↗' Keep 'have to' as 'HAF-tuh'.

drills.targetText: We don't have to come on Saturday.
drills.focus: Expressing no obligation with 'don't have to'
drills.hint: Stress 'don't' slightly to show there is NO obligation. Say 'don't have to' smoothly: 'dohnt-HAF-tuh'.

drills.targetText: You must be quiet in the library.
drills.phonetic: /juː mʌst biː ˈkwaɪ.ət ɪn ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i/
drills.focus: Stress on 'must' and clear pronunciation of 'quiet' and 'library'
drills.hint: 'Quiet' has two syllables: 'KWAI-uht'. 'Library' has three syllables: 'LY-bruh-ree'. Use falling intonation at the end.

roleplay.context: You are practising with Mr. Khoirul about rules in different public places. Mr. Khoirul asks you about rules at school, in the library, and at the hospital. You answer using 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', or 'don't have to'.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! Today we're talking about rules in public places. Let's start with a simple question: What's one rule at school?
turns.translation: Halo! Hari ini kita akan berbicara tentang aturan di tempat umum. Mari kita mulai dengan pertanyaan sederhana: Apa satu aturan di sekolah?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: We must wear uniforms at school.
turns.translation: Kita harus memakai seragam di sekolah.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Perfect! Now tell me, can you use your phone during lessons?
turns.translation: Sempurna! Sekarang beritahu saya, bolehkah kamu menggunakan teleponmu selama pelajaran?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, we mustn't use our phones during lessons.
turns.translation: Tidak, kita tidak boleh menggunakan telepon selama pelajaran.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Excellent! What about homework? Is it necessary to do it every day?
turns.translation: Bagus sekali! Bagaimana dengan pekerjaan rumah? Apakah perlu mengerjakannya setiap hari?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, I have to do my homework every day.
turns.translation: Ya, saya harus mengerjakan pekerjaan rumah saya setiap hari.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Great job! Last question: Do you have to come to school on Sunday?
turns.translation: Kerja bagus! Pertanyaan terakhir: Apakah kamu harus datang ke sekolah pada hari Minggu?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, I don't have to come to school on Sunday.
turns.translation: Tidak, saya tidak harus datang ke sekolah pada hari Minggu.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about the rules at your school. Use the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds. Use 'must', 'mustn't', and 'have to' in your story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell a story! Imagine you are explaining your school rules to a new student. Talk about what students must do, what they mustn't do, and what they have to do every day. Use the three points to help you.
storyPoints: Talk about one thing students must do at school, for example wearing a uniform.
Talk about one thing students mustn't do, for example using phones in class.
Talk about one thing students have to do every day, for example doing homework.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: At my school, we must wear uniforms. We mustn't use our phones in class. We also have to do homework every day.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ət maɪ skuːl wiː mʌst weər ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːmz. wiː ˈmʌs.ənt juːz aʊər fəʊnz ɪn klɑːs. wiː ˈɔːl.səʊ ˈhæf.tə duː ˈhəʊm.wɜːk ˈev.ri deɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use falling intonation when you state each rule. Say 'mustn't' as 'MUSS-nt' and 'have to' as 'HAF-tuh'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using obligation modals in connected speech. Each story point targets a different modal: 'must' for obligation, 'mustn't' for prohibition, and 'have to' for necessity.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about the rules in a hospital. Use the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds. Use 'must', 'mustn't', and 'don't have to' in your story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Great! Now imagine you are visiting a hospital. Tell me about the rules there. What must visitors do? What mustn't they do? What don't they have to do? Use the three points below.
storyPoints: Talk about one thing visitors must do at the hospital, for example being quiet.
Talk about one thing visitors mustn't do, for example smoking.
Talk about one thing visitors don't have to do, for example wearing a uniform.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: At the hospital, visitors must be quiet. They mustn't smoke inside. They don't have to wear a uniform.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ət ðə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ˈvɪz.ɪ.tərz mʌst biː ˈkwaɪ.ət. ðeɪ ˈmʌs.ənt sməʊk ɪnˈsaɪd. ðeɪ dəʊnt ˈhæf.tə weər ə ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Speak slowly and clearly. Stress the modal verbs: 'MUST be quiet', 'MUSTN'T smoke', 'DON'T have to wear'. Use falling intonation for each rule.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task extends obligation language to a hospital setting. It practises the contrast between 'mustn't' (prohibition) and 'don't have to' (no obligation), which is an important distinction for A1 learners.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are a new student at a school. Mr. Khoirul is the teacher. He asks you about school rules. Answer his questions using 'must' or 'mustn't'. Speak naturally and clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to your new school! I am Mr. Khoirul, your teacher. I want to check if you know the school rules. Are you ready? Let me ask you some questions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a new student on your first day at school. Your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, wants to make sure you understand the important school rules. He will ask you about uniforms, being on time, and behaviour in class.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a new student. You are polite and you know the basic school rules. Answer Mr. Khoirul's questions using 'must' or 'mustn't' to show you understand the rules.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I must wear a uniform. I mustn't be late for class.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ mʌst weər ə ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːm. aɪ ˈmʌs.ənt biː leɪt fɔːr klɑːs/
practicumQuestions.hint: When Mr. Khoirul asks about a rule, answer with 'I must...' or 'I mustn't...' Keep your answers short and clear.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises responding to questions about obligations using 'must' and 'mustn't' in a natural school conversation context.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are visiting a library. Mr. Khoirul is the librarian. He explains the library rules. Ask him questions using 'Do I have to...?' and respond to his rules.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Welcome to the city library. I am the librarian. Before you go inside, let me tell you some rules. You can also ask me questions if you are not sure about something.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at a public library for the first time. The librarian, Mr. Khoirul, is explaining the rules to you. You need to ask about what you have to do and what you mustn't do in the library.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a visitor at the library. You are curious and polite. Ask questions like 'Do I have to...?' and respond with 'I understand, I must...' or 'OK, I mustn't...'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Do I have to show my library card? OK, I mustn't eat in the library.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /duː aɪ ˈhæf.tə ʃəʊ maɪ ˈlaɪ.brər.i kɑːd? əʊˈkeɪ aɪ ˈmʌs.ənt iːt ɪn ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use rising intonation when asking 'Do I have to...? ↗' Use falling intonation when confirming a rule: 'I mustn't eat here. ↘'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises asking about obligations with 'Do I have to...?' and confirming understanding of prohibitions with 'mustn't'. It builds question-and-answer fluency.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at an airport. Mr. Khoirul is the security officer. He tells you the rules. Respond and ask questions about what you must do and what you don't have to do.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning, passenger. I am the security officer. Before you go through security, I need to tell you some important rules. Please listen carefully and ask me if you have any questions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a passenger at the airport, going through security. The security officer, Mr. Khoirul, explains the rules about bags, liquids, and documents. You need to show you understand the rules.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a passenger at the airport. You are a little nervous because it is your first time flying. Ask polite questions and confirm you understand the rules using 'must', 'have to', and 'don't have to'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I must show my passport. Do I have to take off my shoes? I don't have to remove my watch.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ mʌst ʃəʊ maɪ ˈpɑːs.pɔːt. duː aɪ ˈhæf.tə teɪk ɒf maɪ ʃuːz? aɪ dəʊnt ˈhæf.tə rɪˈmuːv maɪ wɒtʃ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Practise the difference: 'must' = it is very important. 'Have to' = it is necessary. 'Don't have to' = it is NOT necessary, but you can if you want.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This airport scenario practises all three modal structures in a real-life situation. It helps learners distinguish between obligation (must/have to), prohibition (mustn't), and no obligation (don't have to).

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are a tour guide at a museum. Mr. Khoirul is a tourist. Tell him the museum rules using 'must', 'mustn't', and 'don't have to'. Answer his questions politely.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! I am a tourist visiting this museum. Can you tell me the rules here? What must I do? What mustn't I do? I want to make sure I follow all the rules.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are working as a tour guide at a local museum. A tourist, Mr. Khoirul, has just arrived and wants to know the rules before he starts his visit. You need to explain the rules clearly.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a friendly tour guide at the museum. You explain rules clearly and politely. Use 'You must...', 'You mustn't...', and 'You don't have to...' to help the tourist understand.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You must buy a ticket. You mustn't touch the paintings. You don't have to take a guided tour.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː mʌst baɪ ə ˈtɪk.ɪt. juː ˈmʌs.ənt tʌtʃ ðə ˈpeɪn.tɪŋz. juː dəʊnt ˈhæf.tə teɪk ə ˈɡaɪ.dɪd tʊər/
practicumQuestions.hint: As a tour guide, speak slowly and clearly. Stress the modal verbs so the tourist understands what is required and what is not allowed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay reverses the dynamic – the learner gives rules instead of receiving them. This builds confidence in using obligation language actively and practises all three modal forms.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing the key vocabulary words clearly: 'obligation', 'forbidden', and 'allowed'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's practise some important vocabulary for talking about rules. Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the words 'obligation', 'forbidden', and 'allowed'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It is an obligation to follow the rules. Smoking is forbidden. Talking is not allowed.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt ɪz ən ˌɒb.lɪˈɡeɪ.ʃən tə ˈfɒl.əʊ ðə ruːlz. ˈsməʊ.kɪŋ ɪz fəˈbɪd.ən. ˈtɔː.kɪŋ ɪz nɒt əˈlaʊd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Say 'obligation' as 'ob-li-GAY-shun' with stress on the third syllable. Say 'forbidden' as 'fuh-BID-un' with stress on the second syllable. Say 'allowed' as 'uh-LOUD' with stress on the second syllable.
practicumQuestions.explanation: These vocabulary words are important for understanding and discussing rules at a higher level. Even at A1, exposure to these words helps build recognition. Focus on clear syllable stress.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say these three sentences out loud. Each sentence uses a different grammar structure for rules. Focus on the correct form of each modal verb.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise the grammar of obligation. I want you to say three sentences. The first uses 'must', the second uses 'mustn't', and the third uses 'have to'. Listen to the grammar carefully.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Students must arrive on time. They mustn't cheat on exams. They have to bring their books every day.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈstjuː.dənts mʌst əˈraɪv ɒn taɪm. ðeɪ ˈmʌs.ənt tʃiːt ɒn ɪɡˈzæmz. ðeɪ ˈhæf.tə brɪŋ ðeər bʊks ˈev.ri deɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Notice the grammar pattern: 'must + base verb' (must arrive), 'mustn't + base verb' (mustn't cheat), 'have to + base verb' (have to bring). Never add '-s' or '-ing' after these modals.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill reinforces the grammar rule that modal verbs (must, mustn't) and 'have to' are always followed by the base form of the verb. Speaking these patterns aloud helps build automatic grammatical accuracy.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following words and sentences out loud. Pay careful attention to which syllable is stressed in each word. The stressed syllable is written in CAPITAL letters.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's work on syllable stress. I will show you some words related to rules and obligations. Say each word and sentence clearly, making the stressed syllable louder and longer than the others.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You must follow the rules. It is an ob-li-GA-tion. It is for-BID-den. It is not al-LOWED. It is NE-ces-sa-ry.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː mʌst ˈfɒl.əʊ ðə ruːlz. ɪt ɪz ən ˌɒb.lɪˈɡeɪ.ʃən. ɪt ɪz fəˈbɪd.ən. ɪt ɪz nɒt əˈlaʊd. ɪt ɪz ˈnes.ə.sər.i/
practicumQuestions.hint: Stress patterns: 'FOL-low', 'ob-li-GA-tion' (stress on 3rd syllable), 'for-BID-den' (stress on 2nd syllable), 'al-LOWED' (stress on 2nd syllable), 'NE-ces-sa-ry' (stress on 1st syllable). Make the stressed syllable louder and longer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Correct syllable stress is essential for being understood. English listeners rely on stress patterns to recognise words. Placing stress on the wrong syllable can make a word unrecognisable, even if all the sounds are correct.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentences out loud. Use FALLING intonation (↘) for rule statements and RISING intonation (↗) for yes/no questions. Pay attention to how your voice moves at the end of each sentence.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise intonation. When you state a rule, your voice should go DOWN at the end. When you ask a yes/no question about a rule, your voice should go UP at the end. Say each sentence with the correct intonation.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You must wear a seatbelt. ↘ Do I have to show my ticket? ↗ You mustn't park here. ↘ Do we have to wait? ↗
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː mʌst weər ə ˈsiːt.belt ↘ duː aɪ ˈhæf.tə ʃəʊ maɪ ˈtɪk.ɪt ↗ juː ˈmʌs.ənt pɑːk hɪər ↘ duː wiː ˈhæf.tə weɪt ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: For statements like 'You must wear a seatbelt', let your voice fall naturally at the end, like you are finishing a thought. For questions like 'Do I have to show my ticket?', let your voice rise at the end, like you are waiting for an answer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation carries meaning in English. Falling intonation signals a complete statement or a firm rule. Rising intonation signals a yes/no question. Using the wrong intonation can confuse listeners about whether you are telling or asking.

reading.question: In the passage, Mr. Adams says students must be quiet in the library. What does 'must be quiet' mean?
options: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
It is a suggestion — students can be quiet if they want.
It is not important — students can talk if they want.
reading.answer: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
reading.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong obligation. When Mr. Adams says 'You must be quiet in the library,' he means it is a rule that all students need to follow. Being quiet in the library is required, not optional.

reading.question: The passage says: 'You don't have to bring lunch from home.' What does this mean?
options: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
Bringing lunch from home is forbidden. You must buy food at school.
You must bring lunch from home every day.
reading.answer: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
reading.explanation: 'Don't have to' means something is NOT necessary — it is optional. Students can bring lunch if they want, but they can also buy food at the school cafeteria. It is their choice!

reading.question: Which of these is a PROHIBITION (something you cannot do) mentioned in the passage?
options: You mustn't run near the pool.
You don't have to bring your own towel.
You have to finish your homework.
reading.answer: You mustn't run near the pool.
reading.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a prohibition — something that is forbidden. Running near the pool is not allowed because it is dangerous. 'Don't have to' (option B) means not necessary, and 'have to' (option C) means an obligation, not a prohibition.

reading.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to which place?
reading.explanation: In the passage, Mr. Adams talks about the library rules. He says: 'You must be quiet in the library. You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to the library, which was mentioned in the sentence before.

reading.question: A sign says: 'You must shower before entering the pool.' Which sentence has the SAME meaning?
options: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
You don't have to shower. It is your choice.
You mustn't shower at the pool.
reading.answer: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
reading.explanation: Both 'must' and 'have to' can express obligation. 'You must shower' and 'You have to take a shower' have the same meaning here — showering before swimming is a rule that everyone needs to follow.

reading.question: At the end of the passage, Rina thinks: 'There are rules everywhere!' Why does she think this?

reading.question: What is the difference between 'You mustn't eat here' and 'You don't have to eat here'?
options: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.

reading.answer: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
reading.explanation: This is a very important difference! 'Mustn't' = prohibition (you cannot do it). 'Don't have to' = not necessary (you can choose). 'You mustn't eat here' means eating is NOT allowed. 'You don't have to eat here' means you can eat here if you want, but it is not required.

questions.question: In the passage, Mr. Adams says students must be quiet in the library. What does 'must be quiet' mean?
options: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
It is a suggestion — students can be quiet if they want.
It is not important — students can talk if they want.
questions.answer: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong obligation. When Mr. Adams says 'You must be quiet in the library,' he means it is a rule that all students need to follow. Being quiet in the library is required, not optional.

questions.question: The passage says: 'You don't have to bring lunch from home.' What does this mean?
options: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
Bringing lunch from home is forbidden. You must buy food at school.
You must bring lunch from home every day.
questions.answer: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
questions.explanation: 'Don't have to' means something is NOT necessary — it is optional. Students can bring lunch if they want, but they can also buy food at the school cafeteria. It is their choice!

questions.question: Which of these is a PROHIBITION (something you cannot do) mentioned in the passage?
options: You mustn't run near the pool.
You don't have to bring your own towel.
You have to finish your homework.
questions.answer: You mustn't run near the pool.
questions.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a prohibition — something that is forbidden. Running near the pool is not allowed because it is dangerous. 'Don't have to' (option B) means not necessary, and 'have to' (option C) means an obligation, not a prohibition.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to which place?
questions.answer: The library

questions.question: A sign says: 'You must shower before entering the pool.' Which sentence has the SAME meaning?
options: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
You don't have to shower. It is your choice.
You mustn't shower at the pool.
questions.answer: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
questions.explanation: Both 'must' and 'have to' can express obligation. 'You must shower' and 'You have to take a shower' have the same meaning here — showering before swimming is a rule that everyone needs to follow.

questions.question: At the end of the passage, Rina thinks: 'There are rules everywhere!' Why does she think this?
options: Because she finds rules both at school and at the swimming pool.
Because she does not like any rules.
Because there are no rules at the swimming pool.
questions.answer: Because she finds rules both at school and at the swimming pool.
questions.explanation: Rina learns rules at two different places on the same day — at her new school and at the swimming pool. She notices that rules exist in many places in daily life, so she thinks 'There are rules everywhere!'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence about the school rules in the passage:

Option C is wrong because 'mustn't finish' would mean finishing homework is forbidden, which does not make sense.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'You mustn't eat here' and 'You don't have to eat here'?
options: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
'Don't have to eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Mustn't eat' means eating is optional.
questions.answer: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
questions.explanation: This is a very important difference! 'Mustn't' = prohibition (you cannot do it). 'Don't have to' = not necessary (you can choose). 'You mustn't eat here' means eating is NOT allowed. 'You don't have to eat here' means you can eat here if you want, but it is not required.

questions.characterRole: You are a visitor at the library. You are curious and polite. Ask questions like 'Do I have to...?' and respond with 'I understand, I must...' or 'OK, I mustn't...'

questions.hint: Practise the difference: 'must' = it is very important. 'Have to' = it is necessary. 'Don't have to' = it is NOT necessary, but you can if you want.
questions.explanation: This airport scenario practises all three modal structures in a real-life situation. It helps learners distinguish between obligation (must/have to), prohibition (mustn't), and no obligation (don't have to).

practicumQuestions.question: In the passage, Mr. Adams says students must be quiet in the library. What does 'must be quiet' mean?
options: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
It is a suggestion — students can be quiet if they want.
It is not important — students can talk if they want.
practicumQuestions.answer: It is a strong rule — students need to be silent in the library.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong obligation. When Mr. Adams says 'You must be quiet in the library,' he means it is a rule that all students need to follow. Being quiet in the library is required, not optional.

practicumQuestions.question: The passage says: 'You don't have to bring lunch from home.' What does this mean?
options: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
Bringing lunch from home is forbidden. You must buy food at school.
You must bring lunch from home every day.
practicumQuestions.answer: Bringing lunch from home is not necessary. You can buy food at school.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Don't have to' means something is NOT necessary — it is optional. Students can bring lunch if they want, but they can also buy food at the school cafeteria. It is their choice!

practicumQuestions.question: Which of these is a PROHIBITION (something you cannot do) mentioned in the passage?
options: You mustn't run near the pool.
You don't have to bring your own towel.
You have to finish your homework.
practicumQuestions.answer: You mustn't run near the pool.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a prohibition — something that is forbidden. Running near the pool is not allowed because it is dangerous. 'Don't have to' (option B) means not necessary, and 'have to' (option C) means an obligation, not a prohibition.

practicumQuestions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to which place?
practicumQuestions.explanation: In the passage, Mr. Adams talks about the library rules. He says: 'You must be quiet in the library. You mustn't use your phone there.' The word 'there' refers to the library, which was mentioned in the sentence before.

practicumQuestions.question: A sign says: 'You must shower before entering the pool.' Which sentence has the SAME meaning?
options: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
You don't have to shower. It is your choice.
You mustn't shower at the pool.
practicumQuestions.answer: You have to take a shower before you swim. It is a rule.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Both 'must' and 'have to' can express obligation. 'You must shower' and 'You have to take a shower' have the same meaning here — showering before swimming is a rule that everyone needs to follow.

practicumQuestions.question: At the end of the passage, Rina thinks: 'There are rules everywhere!' Why does she think this?
options: Because she finds rules both at school and at the swimming pool.
Because she does not like any rules.
Because there are no rules at the swimming pool.
practicumQuestions.answer: Because she finds rules both at school and at the swimming pool.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Rina learns rules at two different places on the same day — at her new school and at the swimming pool. She notices that rules exist in many places in daily life, so she thinks 'There are rules everywhere!'

practicumQuestions.question: Choose the correct sentence about the school rules in the passage:
options: Students have to finish their homework before the deadline.
Students don't have to wear a uniform.
practicumQuestions.answer: Students have to finish their homework before the deadline.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The passage clearly states: 'You have to finish your homework before the deadline.' This is an obligation. Option B is wrong because students MUST wear a uniform. Option C is wrong because 'mustn't finish' would mean finishing homework is forbidden, which does not make sense.

practicumQuestions.question: What is the difference between 'You mustn't eat here' and 'You don't have to eat here'?
options: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
'Don't have to eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Mustn't eat' means eating is optional.
practicumQuestions.answer: 'Mustn't eat' means eating is forbidden. 'Don't have to eat' means eating is not necessary but allowed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This is a very important difference! 'Mustn't' = prohibition (you cannot do it). 'Don't have to' = not necessary (you can choose). 'You mustn't eat here' means eating is NOT allowed. 'You don't have to eat here' means you can eat here if you want, but it is not required.

practicumQuestions.question: What is Jamie's nationality?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Jamie is from Spain, so his nationality is Spanish.

practicumQuestions.question: Which sentence is the correct negative form of 'She likes coffee'?
practicumQuestions.explanation: For third person singular (she/he/it), we use 'doesn't + base verb'.

practicumQuestions.question: Where do they usually eat dinner on weekdays?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Daily routines typically describe having dinner at home with family.

practicumQuestions.question: What time does the train to London depart?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Buy' is an irregular verb whose past simple form is 'bought'.

practicumQuestions.question: What does Maria do every Saturday morning?
practicumQuestions.explanation: A routine action in the simple present tense describing Saturday morning.

practicumQuestions.question: Which question is grammatically correct?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Standard question order: Question Word + Auxiliary (do) + Subject (you) + Verb (live).

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 3 sentences about rules in a swimming pool. Use 'must' in one sentence, 'mustn't' in one sentence, and 'have to' in one sentence.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Each sentence uses the correct modal verb or phrase. The base form of the verb follows 'must', 'mustn't', or 'have to'. Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a period. The rules make sense for a swimming pool.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: You must take a shower before you swim. You mustn't run near the pool. Children have to stay with an adult.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Your friend is new at your school. Write a short paragraph (at least 4 sentences) telling your friend about the school rules. Use 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', and 'don't have to' at least once each.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The paragraph has at least 4 sentences. It uses 'must', 'mustn't', 'have to', and 'don't have to' correctly. All verbs after these modals are in base form. Sentences have correct capitalization and punctuation. The content is about school rules.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Welcome to our school! You must wear a uniform every day. You mustn't bring food into the classroom. You have to do your homework every night. You don't have to join a sports club, but it is fun.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 4 sentences about rules on a bus. Use 'must', 'mustn't', 'has to', and 'don't have to'. One sentence should be about the bus driver.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Four sentences are written. 'Must', 'mustn't', 'has to', and 'don't have to' are each used once. 'Has to' is used correctly with a third person singular subject (for example, the bus driver). All verbs after modals are in base form. Correct capitalization and punctuation are used throughout.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Passengers must sit down when the bus is moving. You mustn't talk to the bus driver. The bus driver has to stop at every bus stop. You don't have to buy a ticket online because you can pay on the bus.

Mark does not work in an office downtown.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Dalam present simple, subjek orang ketiga tunggal menggunakan 'doesn't + base verb'.

targetAnswers: They went to the beach on Sunday.
They went to the beach.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Go' adalah kata kerja tidak beraturan yang berubah menjadi 'went' di waktu lampau.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Buat kalimat tanya dari kata-kata berikut:
practicumQuestions.hint: Awali dengan 'Do'.
targetAnswers: Do you like Italian food?
Do you like Italian food
practicumQuestions.explanation: Pola pertanyaan present simple: Do + you + like + objek?

practicumQuestions.instruction: Perbaiki kesalahan tata bahasa dalam kalimat ini:
practicumQuestions.prompt: She don't have any brothers or sisters.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about the rules at your school. Use the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds. Use 'must', 'mustn't', and 'have to' in your story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell a story! Imagine you are explaining your school rules to a new student. Talk about what students must do, what they mustn't do, and what they have to do every day. Use the three points to help you.
storyPoints: Talk about one thing students must do at school, for example wearing a uniform.
Talk about one thing students mustn't do, for example using phones in class.
Talk about one thing students have to do every day, for example doing homework.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: At my school, we must wear uniforms. We mustn't use our phones in class. We also have to do homework every day.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ət maɪ skuːl wiː mʌst weər ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːmz. wiː ˈmʌs.ənt juːz aʊər fəʊnz ɪn klɑːs. wiː ˈɔːl.səʊ ˈhæf.tə duː ˈhəʊm.wɜːk ˈev.ri deɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use falling intonation when you state each rule. Say 'mustn't' as 'MUSS-nt' and 'have to' as 'HAF-tuh'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using obligation modals in connected speech. Each story point targets a different modal: 'must' for obligation, 'mustn't' for prohibition, and 'have to' for necessity.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about the rules in a hospital. Use the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds. Use 'must', 'mustn't', and 'don't have to' in your story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Great! Now imagine you are visiting a hospital. Tell me about the rules there. What must visitors do? What mustn't they do? What don't they have to do? Use the three points below.
storyPoints: Talk about one thing visitors must do at the hospital, for example being quiet.
Talk about one thing visitors mustn't do, for example smoking.
Talk about one thing visitors don't have to do, for example wearing a uniform.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: At the hospital, visitors must be quiet. They mustn't smoke inside. They don't have to wear a uniform.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ət ðə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ˈvɪz.ɪ.tərz mʌst biː ˈkwaɪ.ət. ðeɪ ˈmʌs.ənt sməʊk ɪnˈsaɪd. ðeɪ dəʊnt ˈhæf.tə weər ə ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Speak slowly and clearly. Stress the modal verbs: 'MUST be quiet', 'MUSTN'T smoke', 'DON'T have to wear'. Use falling intonation for each rule.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task extends obligation language to a hospital setting. It practises the contrast between 'mustn't' (prohibition) and 'don't have to' (no obligation), which is an important distinction for A1 learners.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are a new student at a school. Mr. Khoirul is the teacher. He asks you about school rules. Answer his questions using 'must' or 'mustn't'. Speak naturally and clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to your new school! I am Mr. Khoirul, your teacher. I want to check if you know the school rules. Are you ready? Let me ask you some questions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a new student on your first day at school. Your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, wants to make sure you understand the important school rules. He will ask you about uniforms, being on time, and behaviour in class.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a new student. You are polite and you know the basic school rules. Answer Mr. Khoirul's questions using 'must' or 'mustn't' to show you understand the rules.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I must wear a uniform. I mustn't be late for class.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ mʌst weər ə ˈjuː.nɪ.fɔːm. aɪ ˈmʌs.ənt biː leɪt fɔːr klɑːs/
practicumQuestions.hint: When Mr. Khoirul asks about a rule, answer with 'I must...' or 'I mustn't...' Keep your answers short and clear.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises responding to questions about obligations using 'must' and 'mustn't' in a natural school conversation context.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are visiting a library. Mr. Khoirul is the librarian. He explains the library rules. Ask him questions using 'Do I have to...?' and respond to his rules.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Welcome to the city library. I am the librarian. Before you go inside, let me tell you some rules. You can also ask me questions if you are not sure about something.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at a public library for the first time. The librarian, Mr. Khoirul, is explaining the rules to you. You need to ask about what you have to do and what you mustn't do in the library.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a visitor at the library. You are curious and polite. Ask questions like 'Do I have to...?' and respond with 'I understand, I must...' or 'OK, I mustn't...'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Do I have to show my library card? OK, I mustn't eat in the library.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /duː aɪ ˈhæf.tə ʃəʊ maɪ ˈlaɪ.brər.i kɑːd? əʊˈkeɪ aɪ ˈmʌs.ənt iːt ɪn ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use rising intonation when asking 'Do I have to...? ↗' Use falling intonation when confirming a rule: 'I mustn't eat here. ↘'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises asking about obligations with 'Do I have to...?' and confirming understanding of prohibitions with 'mustn't'. It builds question-and-answer fluency.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at an airport. Mr. Khoirul is the security officer. He tells you the rules. Respond and ask questions about what you must do and what you don't have to do.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning, passenger. I am the security officer. Before you go through security, I need to tell you some important rules. Please listen carefully and ask me if you have any questions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a passenger at the airport, going through security. The security officer, Mr. Khoirul, explains the rules about bags, liquids, and documents. You need to show you understand the rules.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a passenger at the airport. You are a little nervous because it is your first time flying. Ask polite questions and confirm you understand the rules using 'must', 'have to', and 'don't have to'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I must show my passport. Do I have to take off my shoes? I don't have to remove my watch.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ mʌst ʃəʊ maɪ ˈpɑːs.pɔːt. duː aɪ ˈhæf.tə teɪk ɒf maɪ ʃuːz? aɪ dəʊnt ˈhæf.tə rɪˈmuːv maɪ wɒtʃ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Practise the difference: 'must' = it is very important. 'Have to' = it is necessary. 'Don't have to' = it is NOT necessary, but you can if you want.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This airport scenario practises all three modal structures in a real-life situation. It helps learners distinguish between obligation (must/have to), prohibition (mustn't), and no obligation (don't have to).

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are a tour guide at a museum. Mr. Khoirul is a tourist. Tell him the museum rules using 'must', 'mustn't', and 'don't have to'. Answer his questions politely.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! I am a tourist visiting this museum. Can you tell me the rules here? What must I do? What mustn't I do? I want to make sure I follow all the rules.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are working as a tour guide at a local museum. A tourist, Mr. Khoirul, has just arrived and wants to know the rules before he starts his visit. You need to explain the rules clearly.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a friendly tour guide at the museum. You explain rules clearly and politely. Use 'You must...', 'You mustn't...', and 'You don't have to...' to help the tourist understand.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You must buy a ticket. You mustn't touch the paintings. You don't have to take a guided tour.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː mʌst baɪ ə ˈtɪk.ɪt. juː ˈmʌs.ənt tʌtʃ ðə ˈpeɪn.tɪŋz. juː dəʊnt ˈhæf.tə teɪk ə ˈɡaɪ.dɪd tʊər/
practicumQuestions.hint: As a tour guide, speak slowly and clearly. Stress the modal verbs so the tourist understands what is required and what is not allowed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay reverses the dynamic – the learner gives rules instead of receiving them. This builds confidence in using obligation language actively and practises all three modal forms.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing the key vocabulary words clearly: 'obligation', 'forbidden', and 'allowed'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's practise some important vocabulary for talking about rules. Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the words 'obligation', 'forbidden', and 'allowed'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It is an obligation to follow the rules. Smoking is forbidden. Talking is not allowed.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt ɪz ən ˌɒb.lɪˈɡeɪ.ʃən tə ˈfɒl.əʊ ðə ruːlz. ˈsməʊ.kɪŋ ɪz fəˈbɪd.ən. ˈtɔː.kɪŋ ɪz nɒt əˈlaʊd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Say 'obligation' as 'ob-li-GAY-shun' with stress on the third syllable. Say 'forbidden' as 'fuh-BID-un' with stress on the second syllable. Say 'allowed' as 'uh-LOUD' with stress on the second syllable.
practicumQuestions.explanation: These vocabulary words are important for understanding and discussing rules at a higher level. Even at A1, exposure to these words helps build recognition. Focus on clear syllable stress.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say these three sentences out loud. Each sentence uses a different grammar structure for rules. Focus on the correct form of each modal verb.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise the grammar of obligation. I want you to say three sentences. The first uses 'must', the second uses 'mustn't', and the third uses 'have to'. Listen to the grammar carefully.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Students must arrive on time. They mustn't cheat on exams. They have to bring their books every day.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈstjuː.dənts mʌst əˈraɪv ɒn taɪm. ðeɪ ˈmʌs.ənt tʃiːt ɒn ɪɡˈzæmz. ðeɪ ˈhæf.tə brɪŋ ðeər bʊks ˈev.ri deɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Notice the grammar pattern: 'must + base verb' (must arrive), 'mustn't + base verb' (mustn't cheat), 'have to + base verb' (have to bring). Never add '-s' or '-ing' after these modals.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill reinforces the grammar rule that modal verbs (must, mustn't) and 'have to' are always followed by the base form of the verb. Speaking these patterns aloud helps build automatic grammatical accuracy.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following words and sentences out loud. Pay careful attention to which syllable is stressed in each word. The stressed syllable is written in CAPITAL letters.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's work on syllable stress. I will show you some words related to rules and obligations. Say each word and sentence clearly, making the stressed syllable louder and longer than the others.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You must follow the rules. It is an ob-li-GA-tion. It is for-BID-den. It is not al-LOWED. It is NE-ces-sa-ry.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː mʌst ˈfɒl.əʊ ðə ruːlz. ɪt ɪz ən ˌɒb.lɪˈɡeɪ.ʃən. ɪt ɪz fəˈbɪd.ən. ɪt ɪz nɒt əˈlaʊd. ɪt ɪz ˈnes.ə.sər.i/
practicumQuestions.hint: Stress patterns: 'FOL-low', 'ob-li-GA-tion' (stress on 3rd syllable), 'for-BID-den' (stress on 2nd syllable), 'al-LOWED' (stress on 2nd syllable), 'NE-ces-sa-ry' (stress on 1st syllable). Make the stressed syllable louder and longer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Correct syllable stress is essential for being understood. English listeners rely on stress patterns to recognise words. Placing stress on the wrong syllable can make a word unrecognisable, even if all the sounds are correct.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentences out loud. Use FALLING intonation (↘) for rule statements and RISING intonation (↗) for yes/no questions. Pay attention to how your voice moves at the end of each sentence.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise intonation. When you state a rule, your voice should go DOWN at the end. When you ask a yes/no question about a rule, your voice should go UP at the end. Say each sentence with the correct intonation.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: You must wear a seatbelt. ↘ Do I have to show my ticket? ↗ You mustn't park here. ↘ Do we have to wait? ↗
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː mʌst weər ə ˈsiːt.belt ↘ duː aɪ ˈhæf.tə ʃəʊ maɪ ˈtɪk.ɪt ↗ juː ˈmʌs.ənt pɑːk hɪər ↘ duː wiː ˈhæf.tə weɪt ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: For statements like 'You must wear a seatbelt', let your voice fall naturally at the end, like you are finishing a thought. For questions like 'Do I have to show my ticket?', let your voice rise at the end, like you are waiting for an answer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation carries meaning in English. Falling intonation signals a complete statement or a firm rule. Rising intonation signals a yes/no question. Using the wrong intonation can confuse listeners about whether you are telling or asking.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Deskripsikan rutinitas pagi harimu dengan kalimat berikut:
practicumQuestions.prompt: Every morning, I wake up at six and drink a hot cup of tea.
practicumQuestions.sampleAnswer: Every morning, I wake up at six and drink a hot cup of tea.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈevri ˈmɔːnɪŋ aɪ weɪk ʌp ət sɪks ənd drɪŋk ə hɒt kʌp əv tiː/

practicumQuestions.instruction: Ucapkan pertanyaan menanyakan arah ke stasiun terdekat:
practicumQuestions.prompt: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the nearest bus station?
practicumQuestions.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the nearest bus station?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪkˈskjuːz miː kʊd juː tel miː haʊ tə get tə ðə ˈnɪərɪst bʌs ˈsteɪʃn/
